routes.description: Jesus identifies himself with a second divine power already present in Jewish scripture, exercises divine prerogatives, and receives the religious treatment appropriate to Yahweh.
routes.successCriteria: Show that Jesus’s sayings, actions, followers, and opponents converge on personal divine identity rather than merely delegated or name-bearing authority.

motionBridge.description: The convergent textual evidence establishes that Jesus personally claimed divine identity.

centralBridges.description: Jewish two-powers traditions make Jesus’s divine self-identification intelligible.
Jesus claims divine prerogatives such as final judgment and resurrection.
Early followers and opponents understood Jesus in distinctively divine terms.

subsidiaryBridges.description: The blasphemy reactions support a divine reading of Jesus’s claims.
Philippians applies Yahweh’s name and universal homage to Jesus.

routes.description: The relevant texts distinguish Jesus from God and better describe a uniquely authorized, divine-name-bearing agent whose powers and honors are delegated and shareable.
routes.successCriteria: Show that unity, authority, glory, judgment, name-bearing, and homage do not uniquely entail identity with Yahweh and that the contrary historical framework is insufficiently established.

motionBridge.description: The texts better support delegated authority and later high christology than Jesus’s personal claim to be Yahweh.

centralBridges.description: Jesus describes his unity with the Father in terms extended to believers.
Jesus receives and passes on authority, glory, judgment, and forgiveness.
Divine name-bearing explains exalted language without identity with Yahweh.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Blasphemy accusations do not uniquely establish a claim to be God.
Proskynesis does not by itself establish cultic worship of Jesus.

sections.title: Two powers and name-bearing
sections.rationale: This framework determines whether the scriptural divine figures establish identity with God or permit an authorized representative interpretation.

sections.title: Claims and blasphemy reactions
sections.rationale: Jesus’s trial language and hostile reactions are central evidence for what his hearers understood him to claim.

sections.title: Unity and delegated prerogatives
sections.rationale: The dispute over shared unity, judgment, life, and glory directly tests whether Jesus’s authority is inherent or delegated.

sections.title: Exaltation and worship
sections.rationale: Early Christian exaltation language and acts of homage materially bear on whether followers treated Jesus as Yahweh.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: Old Testament passages present one God as two distinguishable divine powers, furnishing the Jewish framework in which Jesus identifies himself as one power.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Some of you are familiar with the early Jewish belief in the two powers in heaven. The Old Testament is very clear that there's one true God. But there are numerous passages in the Old Testament where we see two divine figures.

moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduced David Wood immediately before this uninterrupted affirmative opening statement.

response.rationale: This opens the affirmative’s governing historical and interpretive framework without replying to an earlier selected move.

precisionFindings.rationale: The two-powers proposition is recoverable, though the category of a divine figure is not yet sharply delimited.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cited textual pattern supports a live framework, but the move initially presents its historical significance more firmly than demonstrated.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from one God and distinguishable divine figures to a two-powers problem is coherent with a bounded interpretive bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific scriptural patterns support the framework, but this span supplies limited evidence about its first-century prevalence.

responsiveness.rationale: As a constructive opening, it efficiently establishes the affirmative’s adopted framework and intended inferential route.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move materially advances the affirmative’s central two-powers bridge rather than yet completing the motion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move does not yet represent or attack a developed live alternative, so charity is not tested.

moves.evidenceBasis: The move relies on the asserted Old Testament pattern of one God alongside two distinguishable divine figures.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: At his trial Jesus identified himself with Daniel’s cloud-coming Son of Man, prompting a blasphemy judgment because he claimed to be a divine heavenly power.

sourceSpan.excerpt: again the high priest asked him are you the Christ the son of the blessed and Jesus said I am and you will see the son of man seated at the right hand of power and coming with the clouds of heaven and the high priest tore his garments and said what further witnesses do we need you have heard his blasphemy what is your decision and they all condemned him as deserving death

moves.attributionBasis: This passage occurs within David Wood’s continuous opening statement and presents his affirmative interpretation of Mark 14.

response.rationale: The move directly constructs the motion-level inference from Jesus’s words and the high priest’s reaction.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claimed trial inference is clear and textually bounded, although alternative grounds for blasphemy remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The reaction strongly supports an extraordinary claim, but does not alone uniquely identify the alleged offense as identity with Yahweh.

charity.alternative: The reaction could concern an exalted messianic or otherwise blasphemous claim without identity with Yahweh.
charity.decisiveQualification: Blasphemy has a wider possible extension than personally claiming to be God.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument is intelligible, but requires the material bridge that this specific blasphemy reaction uniquely indicates divine identity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The trial text and hostile reaction are specific evidence, though rival explanations of the legal charge remain insufficiently compared.

responsiveness.rationale: As constructive material, it directly advances the central motion through Jesus’s words and contemporaneous reaction.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move expressly supports the complete affirmative conclusion that Jesus personally claimed divine identity.

representationalCharity.rationale: It acknowledges the reaction but compresses the live qualification that blasphemy need not uniquely mean claiming identity with God.

moves.evidenceBasis: The evidence is Mark’s trial narrative, Danielic cloud imagery, the high priest’s garment tearing, and the death judgment.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: Jesus claims Yahweh’s final-judgment role and requires that the Son receive honor just as the Father does.

sourceSpan.excerpt: But in Matthew 25, Jesus declares, "But when the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the angels with him, then he will sit on his glorious throne. All the nations will be gathered before him." He tells us in John 5, "For the Father judges no one but has given all judgment to the Son that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father."

moves.attributionBasis: The passage remains within David Wood’s uninterrupted opening and explicitly develops his divine-prerogatives argument.

response.rationale: This is an independent constructive argument from judgment and equal honor, with no earlier selected target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The judgment and honor claims are clear, while the significance of the Father giving judgment remains an implicit qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The prerogatives strongly support elevated status, but the passage’s delegation language leaves a material caveat.

charity.alternative: The Father delegates judgment to an authorized Son who remains distinct from and subordinate to the giver.
charity.decisiveQualification: The text expressly says judgment is given to the Son.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from final judgment and equivalent honor to divine status is stable, with delegation as one bounded unresolved bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Two specific passages support the claimed prerogatives, though the effect of explicit delegation needs fuller comparison.

responsiveness.rationale: The constructive directly establishes a major affirmative evidential line concerning Jesus’s claimed functions.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move strongly supports the central divine-prerogatives bridge without alone settling every motion-level alternative.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move quotes the giving of judgment but does not fairly develop its importance for the delegated-authority alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The move compares Matthew’s universal judgment scene and John’s language of judgment and honor given to the Son.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: Philippians 2 applies Yahweh’s unique name and Isaiah’s universal homage to Jesus, showing that early Christians placed Jesus within divine identity.

sourceSpan.excerpt: In Philippians 2, Paul quotes an early Christian song or poem or creed about Jesus. God exalted him to the highest place and gave him the name that is above every name, that at the name of Jesus, every knee should bow in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue acknowledged that Jesus Christ is Lord. This is a reference to Isaiah 45.

moves.attributionBasis: David Wood presents this source and interpretation during his continuous opening statement before the opposing opening begins.

response.rationale: The move constructively introduces early Christian exaltation evidence without addressing an earlier selected objection.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition and intertext are clear, though the distinction between receiving the name and inherently possessing it remains implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The Isaiah allusion strongly warrants high christology, but its precise identity implications remain interpretively contested.

charity.alternative: Jesus receives an exalted divine name and delegated homage after obedience rather than being identified as Yahweh inherently.
charity.decisiveQualification: The hymn says God gave Jesus the name and exalted him.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The Isaiah intertext creates a strong inferential route, with the meaning of bestowed name-bearing as the unresolved bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A specific early hymn and identifiable scriptural allusion support the case, though translation and interpretive alternatives remain.

responsiveness.rationale: As constructive evidence, the move substantially develops how Jesus’s followers understood his status.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the necessary subsidiary exaltation bridge rather than the complete motion conclusion by itself.

representationalCharity.rationale: It preserves the hymn’s bestowed-exaltation language but gives little weight to its strongest non-identity interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The evidence is the Philippians hymn’s exaltation, bestowed name, universal bowing, confession, and its Isaiah 45 allusion.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: John 10 shows Jesus answering a divinity accusation with Psalm 82’s non-Yahweh gods, making misunderstanding rather than identity with Yahweh a live reading.

sourceSpan.excerpt: There is one place in the gospels where Jesus is directly accused of claiming to be God. It's in John chapter 10. Jesus responds by saying, "I and the Father are one." The Jewish opponents picked up stones. How does Jesus respond? "Is it not written in your law I have said you are gods?" The psalmist is talking about beings who are not in fact Yahweh and yet are called gods. So it's a misunderstanding.

moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduced Alex O’Connor’s opening, and this passage is part of his uninterrupted opposing presentation.

components.text: Hostile accusations and attempted punishment are treated as reliable indicators that Jesus claimed identity with God.
The reaction must distinguish identity with Yahweh from other exalted or blasphemous claims.

response.rationale: It directly diagnoses hostile misunderstanding through Jesus’s own corrective use of Psalm 82 and states that the accusation therefore does not establish identity.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly distinguishes being called a god from identity with Yahweh and states the proposed consequence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Psalm 82 supports a corrective reading, though declaring the entire episode a misunderstanding goes beyond what the quotation alone fixes.

charity.alternative: Jesus invokes Psalm 82 as a legal defense while still maintaining a unique divine-son claim.
charity.decisiveQualification: The defense may rebut the immediate charge without reducing Jesus to an ordinary human.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The corrective-reading inference is coherent, though it does not exclude a legal defense compatible with a stronger christological claim.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move closely engages a specific textual response and its source psalm, while the exclusivity of its interpretation remains disputed.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts the decisive use of hostile reaction and explicitly states why that evidence can be defeated by misunderstanding.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move attacks the complete affirmative inference that accusation and reaction establish personal divine identity.

representationalCharity.rationale: It accurately presents the divinity reading but somewhat compresses the alternative legal-technical interpretation of Jesus’s answer.

moves.evidenceBasis: The evidence is John 10’s accusation, stoning response, Jesus’s Psalm 82 quotation, and the psalm’s non-Yahweh referents.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Jesus extends his oneness and mutual indwelling with the Father to all believers, so those expressions do not uniquely establish identity with Yahweh.

sourceSpan.excerpt: What does Jesus say in his own words? John 17 20 onwards. I pray also for those who believe in me through their message. That all of them may be one. Father, just as you are in me and I am in you, may they also be in us. If this is supposed to indicate that Jesus is claiming to be identical to Yahweh, what does that make the rest of us?

moves.attributionBasis: This remains within Alex O’Connor’s uninterrupted opening and explicitly answers the affirmative’s treatment of Jesus’s relation to the Father.

components.text: Jesus’s unique relation to the Father is used to support his possession of divine status and prerogatives.
The separate claim that Jesus exercises universal judgment and receives equal honor must also be explained.

response.rationale: The move directly contests uniqueness through John 17 but does not yet answer the selected target’s distinct judgment and honor components.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly limits its inference to unity and indwelling language and supplies the comparison with believers.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The textual parallel warrants the narrower conclusion that unity language alone does not uniquely prove identity.

charity.alternative: Believers participate in unity by grace while the Son possesses a categorically unique relation to the Father.
charity.decisiveQualification: Analogous relational language need not imply identical ontological status.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The shared-language counterexample coherently defeats a simple inference from oneness alone, subject to an ontological-degree distinction.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The same discourse supplies a direct and specific comparison, although the metaphysical equivalence of the relations remains debatable.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts the decisive uniqueness premise but leaves judgment and equal honor, also indispensable to the selected move, unanswered.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move strongly advances the con route’s central shared-unity bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: It fairly states the identity inference but underdevelops the strongest distinction between participatory and intrinsic unity.

moves.evidenceBasis: The evidence is John 17’s prayer that believers be one and mutually included just as Father and Son are one.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Stephen’s execution and broader blasphemy charges show that violent blasphemy reactions do not uniquely establish a claim to be God.

sourceSpan.excerpt: if you look in Acts, Steven is telling the story of the Jews to the Jewish authorities who he's been brought before on charges of blasphemy. He's eventually stoned to death. Sometimes Christians act as if the only way to commit blasphemy is to claim to be God. That is simply not the case. If changing the customs that Moses has handed on to us is enough to get somebody convicted of blasphemy, I'm not sure we should read too deeply into the accusations of blasphemy against Jesus.

moves.attributionBasis: The speaker remains Alex O’Connor in the same opening statement and explicitly returns to David Wood’s blasphemy argument.

components.text: The high priest’s blasphemy finding is offered as evidence of a divine-identity claim.
The reaction must distinguish identity with Yahweh from other possible blasphemous offenses.

response.rationale: The move directly supplies counterexamples to the inference that a blasphemy charge or execution uniquely identifies a claim to be God.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is carefully limited to the non-uniqueness of blasphemy evidence rather than denying all evidential relevance.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cited range of charges adequately supports caution against treating blasphemy as a unique diagnostic.

charity.alternative: The precise timing and content of the reaction may still indicate offense at a uniquely divine claim.
charity.decisiveQualification: Non-uniqueness of blasphemy generally does not settle the meaning of this particular reaction.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counterexample successfully defeats uniqueness, while leaving the contextual inference in the particular trial partly intact.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Acts supplies concrete comparative evidence, though differing contexts limit how decisively it transfers to Jesus’s trial.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts both the reaction evidence and the required uniqueness inference, supplying a clear contrary comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move attacks the necessary subsidiary blasphemy bridge rather than the entire affirmative route alone.

representationalCharity.rationale: It treats the argument as an evidential inference and does not deny that context could make a particular charge more significant.

moves.evidenceBasis: The evidence is Stephen’s blasphemy prosecution, execution, and accusations concerning the temple, law, and Mosaic customs.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Jewish traditions of investing agents with God’s name and authority explain exalted treatment of Jesus without identifying the agent as Yahweh.

sourceSpan.excerpt: this idea of the divine name being invested into people and them having the authority of God without being Yahweh themselves is I think the important ticket here. When every knee will bow to Jesus, what is the context? Jesus has been given the name that is above all other names. Given it. This is a common theme. I don't think it lends too nicely to his interpretation.

moves.attributionBasis: Alex O’Connor is still delivering his opening and explicitly applies the name-bearing model against the prior affirmative interpretation.

components.text: Distinguishable divine figures are taken to be two powers who are both God.
The historical prevalence and precise boundaries of the two-powers framework must be established.
Receiving Yahweh’s name and universal homage is treated as inclusion in divine identity.
The Isaiah allusion’s exclusive divine force must be distinguished from representative name-bearing.

response.rationale: It answers the identity inference with an agentive name-bearing model and directly addresses bestowed name and homage, but not the full historical framework.

precisionFindings.rationale: The name-bearing alternative and its non-identity implication are clearly stated and applied to a specific exaltation text.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The model is offered as the better interpretation rather than as a necessary conclusion, fitting the comparative warrant.

charity.alternative: The unique scope of Jesus’s name, homage, and role exceeds ordinary representative name-bearing.
charity.decisiveQualification: Bestowed language can coexist with inclusion in divine identity under an incarnation framework.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The representative-agent model coherently explains bestowed authority, though its adequacy for the full scope of the evidence remains compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move invokes a recognizable Jewish pattern and the hymn’s wording, but provides limited verification within this selected span.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts the decisive identity inferences but leaves part of the two-powers historical foundation untreated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the con route’s central name-bearing bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: It accurately preserves the affirmative’s emphasis on Jewish context and universal homage while proposing a stronger alternative explanation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The evidence is the Jewish representative-name pattern and Philippians’ express statement that Jesus was given the supreme name.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: Jesus’s Psalm 82 response is a legal objection to an automatic blasphemy conviction, not a denial of his unique divine-son claim.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Jesus answered them, "Is it not written in your law I have said you are gods? If he called them gods to whom the word of God came and scripture cannot be set aside, what about the one whom the father set apart as his very own and sent into the world?" This is not Jesus saying, "you're misunderstanding. I'm just a regular dude." He's using a legal technicality here.

moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduced David Wood’s rebuttal, and this passage expressly answers Alex O’Connor’s Psalm 82 interpretation.

components.text: Jesus’s appeal to Psalm 82 is treated as correcting a mistaken claim that he identified himself with Yahweh.
The non-Yahweh use of gods is offered as the controlling interpretation of Jesus’s own status.

response.rationale: The reply contacts both components and diagnoses the inference as confusing a legal defense against automatic conviction with a retraction of status.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between legal sufficiency and christological retraction is clearly and consistently expressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The immediate argumentative function plausibly supports the stated legal-defense reading without requiring that the passage alone prove divinity.

charity.alternative: Psalm 82 supplies Jesus’s substantive self-classification as a non-Yahweh god or authorized son.
charity.decisiveQualification: A fortiori legal reasoning can invoke lesser gods without equating Jesus’s status with theirs.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The legal-defense interpretation coherently explains why Jesus cites lesser bearers of divine terminology while maintaining a greater claim.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The wording about the uniquely sanctified and sent Son supports the distinction, though broader Johannine context still carries weight.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts the decisive corrective inference and explicitly explains why that inference fails to follow from the legal argument.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The reply attacks the con route’s central name-bearing interpretation of Jesus’s own response.

representationalCharity.rationale: It recognizes the non-Yahweh Psalm referents, although the phrase about being a regular person mildly weakens the opposing position.

moves.evidenceBasis: The evidence is the structure of Jesus’s Psalm 82 argument and his contrast between prior gods and the uniquely set-apart, sent Son.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: John 17 itself distinguishes Jesus from ordinary believers by stating that he shared glory with the Father before the world existed.

sourceSpan.excerpt: John 17:5. And now, Father, glorify me in your presence with the glory I had with you before the world began. Alex quoted John 17 to show that Jesus is just claiming some regular relationship that we can all have with God. What does Jesus say in the same chapter that Alex is quoting? That sounds like Jesus is claiming to have glory with the Father before the world began.

moves.attributionBasis: This remains in David Wood’s rebuttal and explicitly identifies Alex O’Connor’s earlier John 17 argument as its target.

components.text: John 17 extends oneness and mutual indwelling language from Father and Son to believers.
The same-way language is offered to show that Jesus’s relation is not categorically unique.

response.rationale: The reply supplies a strong same-chapter distinction through preexistent glory, but does not directly interpret the shared same-way language.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move makes the limited and clear claim that preexistent glory differentiates Jesus from ordinary believers.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cited verse strongly supports a distinctive preexistent relation, though it does not alone settle ontological identity.

charity.alternative: Pre-world glory can be proleptic, bestowed, or subsequently shared rather than proof of intrinsic deity.
charity.decisiveQualification: The verse’s natural temporal reading depicts glory possessed with the Father before creation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Preexistent shared glory is a coherent counterweight to equivalence with believers, though it does not directly resolve the analogy’s exact scope.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The same chapter provides specific contrary evidence, with residual interpretive questions about preexistence and shared glory.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts the uniqueness issue decisively but leaves the target’s exact same-way and believer-indwelling comparison unanswered.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the con route’s central shared-unity bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: Calling the opposing account a regular relationship understates its express allowance that Jesus occupies a uniquely exalted position.

moves.evidenceBasis: The evidence is John 17:5’s claim of glory possessed with the Father before the world began.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Even the glory Jesus possessed is given to him and then given to the disciples, showing that glory and related prerogatives are delegable rather than identity-exclusive.

sourceSpan.excerpt: David mentioned the glory that's given to Jesus in John 17:5. Let's keep reading John 17 and see what Jesus wants to do with that glory. Jesus says that the glory you've given me, I will give to them. The glory you've given me, I will give to them, the disciples. Jesus is given all of these things, what he then does with those things, and whether he delegates them to other people.

moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduced Alex O’Connor’s rebuttal, and he explicitly responds to David Wood’s immediately prior John 17:5 argument.

components.text: Preexistent glory with the Father is presented as a categorical distinction between Jesus and believers.
The significance of that glory must account for the same chapter’s extension of glory to disciples.

response.rationale: The reply directly addresses the cited glory and supplies the same chapter’s language that it is given to Jesus and passed to disciples.

precisionFindings.rationale: The delegation claim, relevant recipients, and limited consequence for exclusivity are all clearly recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The repeated giving language warrants the conclusion that glory alone is not an identity-exclusive marker.

charity.alternative: The Son can share divine glory derivatively with believers while uniquely possessing it before creation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Sharing a prerogative need not erase a categorical distinction in its mode of possession.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The same-chapter continuation directly challenges exclusivity, while still allowing a distinction between intrinsic and participatory glory.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The reply uses closely connected textual evidence and accurately identifies express giving and onward delegation.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts every indispensable component of the preexistent-glory reply and explains the contrary significance of the continuation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move strongly supports the con route’s central delegation bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: It accurately preserves the pre-world glory claim while arguing that the chapter’s later distribution changes its exclusivity.

moves.evidenceBasis: The evidence is John 17’s description of glory given by the Father to Jesus and then given by Jesus to the disciples.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Proskynesis ordinarily denotes physical prostration before higher authorities and does not uniquely establish cultic worship, so homage to Jesus cannot by itself prove deity.

sourceSpan.excerpt: I suppose I really want to nail down on this worship point. David says, "proskuneo can mean just simply bowing down. But in a religious context, it means something else." How do you know that without begging the question? Why isn't it that people are offering proskuneo worship after Jesus ascends? Because it refers to a physical action. Because it's not referring to worship of the kind that David wants it to be in this context.

moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduced Alex O’Connor’s second rebuttal, and the passage explicitly answers David Wood’s worship and homage line.

components.text: Universal bowing and confession directed to Jesus are treated as divine religious homage.
The bestowed divine name and Isaiah 45 intertext independently strengthen the identity inference.

response.rationale: The reply directly contests the worship inference by distinguishing physical prostration from cultic service, but does not answer the bestowed-name intertext.

precisionFindings.rationale: The lexical distinction and the limited claim that prostration alone is insufficient are clearly expressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The lexical range and distribution warrant caution without asserting that no homage to Jesus could ever be religious.

charity.alternative: Context can elevate proskynesis from ordinary homage to religious worship, especially with divine titles and scriptural allusions.
charity.decisiveQualification: Lexical range does not prevent context from selecting a cultic sense.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The anti-circularity objection and lexical distinction are coherent, while contextual differentiation remains possible.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move’s distributional and lexical considerations support non-uniqueness, though this span does not fully analyze Philippians’ particular context.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts the decisive homage component but leaves the divine-name and Isaiah intertext components unanswered.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move advances the necessary subsidiary worship bridge rather than independently completing the con route.

representationalCharity.rationale: It accurately states the contextual-worship answer and challenges its criterion without reducing it to a purely lexical claim.

moves.evidenceBasis: The evidence is the lexical range of proskynesis, its physical character, and its limited post-ascension distribution in the cited texts.
